coherence.reasons: Both run a clean pyramid from governing thought to evidence. X's is the tighter of the two: four summary claims (cost, limits, options, plan) map one-to-one onto sections and slide titles. Y's economics / constraints / recommended-path structure is equally consistent, and it adds a hypothesis-test slide and a five-test scorecard that feed the recommendation. Each has one small internal tension. X says 'only the cross-dock fee could change the 2029 decision' while elsewhere also requiring proven peak service. Y titles a slide 'waiting beats closing now, even under Reading B' while its own arithmetic shows closing gaining $0.14M over two years, so the claim rests on the risk asymmetry rather than the number. Net difference is negligible.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred answer (keep East, take Option K, test the cross-dock, decide at the 2029 lease) and both reject close-to-Central on cost, service and capacity. Y weighs the alternatives more completely. It treats deferral as an explicit option (D) with a one-time cost, and it specifies a test with no two-year minimum, where X says 'run the cross-dock through the holiday peak' without saying how that avoids the minimum commitment or what it costs. Y sets quantified gate criteria (at least 92% all-ZIP, at least 90% in peak weeks, network at least 93.5%, cost at least $0.2M below K) and sizes a lower-growth case. It also notes that capacity is no argument against the cross-dock, and it flags East's own unstated capacity at 220k and a service guardrail on K's shift changes. X's sensitivity table with switching thresholds is good and its fee-versus-floor point is equally sharp, but its decision gate is less defined and it claims K is 'the only design' passing tests the cross-dock nominally passes on paper.

evidence.reasons: Both get every required calculation right: $1.2M incremental cost, $0.10M net saving, 389,600 against 360,000, and a 90.3% network rate. Both add the 88.3% Eastern break-even, zero saving at 2028 volume, the 7.5-year payback and the $1.85M against the $0.9M budget. Both handle the 98%/96% rural exclusion, the confounded renewal claim and the pilot's limits correctly, and I found no arithmetic errors in either. Y uses the evidence slightly more fully: a whole-network all-in model for 2027 and 2028 with two-year totals, break-even volumes against both K and the status quo, a sized lower-growth capacity case (14.8k over), and both readings of the cross-dock minimum quantified. Its invented inputs (the $0.25M test cap, the 2-point rural haircut) are clearly labelled as assumptions. X's Eastern-only cost view is valid and its 50-cent surcharge break-even is a nice touch, but its lower-growth case is only qualitative and 'only design that passes service, capacity, budget' slightly overstates against a cross-dock that clears them on paper. X also says one written answer on the fee 'decides the 2029 lease', which is stronger than its own evidence supports.

revision.reasons: The key expects 'keep with conditions'. Y tests the CEO's hypothesis explicitly: it breaks it into five conditions, marks each HOLDS or PARTLY, and refines it three ways. Those are optimize rather than merely retain; Central capacity (the CEO's stated reason) only rules out close-to-Central and says nothing about the cross-dock; and keep through 2029, not permanently, with a gate. It also addresses the pack's point that the CEO had not shown East was the cheapest way to meet the SLA, and notes that the corrections cut both ways (the 98% and the loyalty claim inflated the keep case). X arrives at the same conditional retention and corrects the same circulated claims in an appendix, but never engages the CEO's reasoning as a hypothesis or points out that the capacity argument alone is insufficient against the cross-dock.

overall.reasons: Both are accurate, defensible documents that meet all four defensibility criteria and avoid all four traps. X is leaner and its threshold-based sensitivity table is useful. Y serves the board better on the points that make the recommendation executable: explicit decisions requested, a deferral option with a cost, a test structured to avoid the two-year minimum, quantified gate criteria for the 2029 decision, and a sized lower-growth case. It also gives an explicit, balanced verdict on the CEO's hypothesis, including where its reasoning falls short. Y's assumptions are flagged clearly enough that the extra detail does not introduce unsupported claims.
